text: A JVM interprets bytecode at first and compiles hot methods to machine code later. Why not compile everything up front?
choices: Most code runs rarely, compiling costs time, and running first lets the JIT observe actual types and branches before optimising.
Because bytecode verification must complete before compilation, and it runs lazily per method.
Because compiling everything would exceed the memory available for the code cache.
Because ahead-of-time compilation would lose the platform independence bytecode provides.
explanation: The second half is the interesting half. A JIT knows things an ahead-of-time compiler cannot: which branch is usually taken, which type actually arrives at a call site, which method is worth inlining. Chapter 21 measures the payoff — a call site that only ever sees one implementing class gets devirtualized and inlined, and the virtual call disappears entirely.
